content: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 2 (PCK2), also known as PEPCK-M, is a mitochondrial isozyme of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PCK or PEPCK) in humans. It is encoded by the PCK2 gene located on chromosome 14. This gene produces a mitochondrial enzyme that facilitates the conversion of oxaloacetate (OAA) to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) in the presence of guanosine triphosphate (GTP). A cytosolic form of this enzyme, encoded by a different gene, plays a central role in gluconeogenesis in the liver. Additionally, alternative splicing of the PCK2 gene has been observed, resulting in transcript variants. The PCK2 gene encodes the mitochondrial form of PCK and shares 68% DNA sequence homology and 70% amino acid sequence homology with the cytosolic form, PCK1. This structural similarity suggests that PCK2 and PCK1 likely originated from a common ancestral gene. The total length of the PCK2 gene spans approximately 10 kilobases (kb). Unlike PCK1, PCK2 contains Alu sequences in its introns. Furthermore, PCK2 includes an 18-residue mitochondrial targeting sequence at its N-terminal. Regulatory elements, such as five GC boxes and three CCAAT boxes, are located 1819 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site. The proximal promoter region of PCK2 also contains two putative ATF/CRE sequences that bind activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4). As a phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, PCK2 catalyzes the GTP-driven conversion of OAA to PEP, a rate-limiting step in gluconeogenesis. This reaction serves as a critical link between glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates within the mitochondria. In pancreatic β-cells, PCK2 regulates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by recycling GTP generated from the succinyl-CoA synthetase reaction. This process drives the TCA cycle, converting PEP to pyruvate and subsequently to acetyl-CoA for the citrate synthase reaction. Since most glycolytic reactions upstream of PEP and downstream of glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) are reversible, PCK2-mediated PEP synthesis can support various biosynthetic pathways, including serine, glycerol, and nucleotide synthesis. Notably, PCK2 preferentially converts OAA derived from lactate, enabling biosynthesis even under low-glucose conditions. Consequently, PCK2 activity supports cell growth and survival during metabolic stress. While PCK1 is predominantly expressed in the liver and kidney, PCK2 is ubiquitously expressed across various cell types, including leukocytes and neurons, as well as in non-gluconeogenic tissues such as the pancreas, brain, and heart. Unlike PCK1, whose expression is regulated by hormones and nutrients involved in gluconeogenesis, PCK2 is constitutively expressed. These differences suggest that PCK2 may perform additional non-gluconeogenic functions. PCK2 has clinical significance, particularly in its association with several cancers, including lung cancer, where it promotes tumorigenesis through its gluconeogenic function. Under low-glucose conditions, endoplasmic reticulum stress upregulates ATF4, which in turn increases PCK2 expression. By enabling cells to utilize alternative cataplerotic pathways to convert TCA cycle intermediates into glycolytic intermediates, PCK2 activity enhances the survival of tumor cells under glucose-deprived conditions. Given its role in gluconeogenesis, PCK2 deficiency is expected to disrupt glucose homeostasis and lead to hypoglycemia. However, while two cases of PCK2 deficiency have been documented, subsequent studies suggest that PCK2 deficiency may not have been the primary cause in these instances.
